title: Health and money don’t count
text: The Stoics said only one thing is truly good: a good character. Money, health and status are ‘indifferents’. Nice to have, but a crook can have them too.
em: only one thing is truly good
author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 7
more:
Zeno of Citium started teaching this in a painted colonnade in Athens around 300 BC. He split the world in three: good (a good character), bad (a bad character) and everything else.

The Stoics admitted some indifferents are ‘preferred’. Health beats sickness, and you’re allowed to go after it. But no outside thing can make you a good person or stop you being one. So for a Stoic, a missed promotion can’t hurt you. Cheating to get one can.

text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. … Not in our power are the body, property, reputation … whatever are not our own acts.
author: Epictetus
more:
This is the first line of the Encheiridion, or ‘handbook’, a short summary of Epictetus’s teaching put together by his student Arrian. He sorts everything into two piles. Your judgments, intentions and desires are yours. Your body, your money and what people think of you are finally up to the world.

Most daily stress comes from mixing up the piles, like trying to control someone’s opinion of you while ignoring your own response to it.

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible…
em: by the opinions about the things
author: Epictetus
more:
Epictetus splits every upset into two steps. Something happens, then you add a story about it. This is a disaster. That was an insult. Most of the suffering lives in the story.

Pain is still real for him. But there’s more room than you’d think between what happens and how you take it. Cognitive behavioural therapy grew partly out of the same idea, and its founders credited the Stoics.

text: …nothing ought to be unexpected by us. … we should consider, not what is wont to happen, but what can happen.
author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 91 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1920)
more:
Seneca wrote this after a fire destroyed the city of Lyon in a single night, leaving a friend of his badly shaken. His advice became a Stoic exercise later called premeditatio malorum, rehearsing in your head what could go wrong.

Oddly, the goal is calm. If you’ve already pictured losing a job or a plan falling apart, the real thing finds you ready. And picturing the loss reminds you what you have now.

text: …wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
author: Epictetus
more:
Epictetus isn’t telling you to stop trying. Work for the outcome you want. But once the result is in, arguing with it only adds a second injury to the first.

‘Tranquil flow of life’ echoes an old Stoic definition of happiness: a life that flows smoothly, like a river going around rocks. Centuries later Nietzsche praised a similar attitude and called it amor fati, love of fate.

title: Pull your circles closer
text: Hierocles pictured you at the centre of rings: family, relatives, neighbours, city, all humanity. His exercise was to keep pulling the outer rings inward.
author: Hierocles
source: Hierocles, Elements of Ethics (fragment preserved by Stobaeus)
more:
Hierocles was a Stoic of the 2nd century AD, and he shows the side of Stoicism people forget. If virtue is the only good, then justice and kindness to others sit at the core. The Stoics called themselves citizens of the world.

The circles make that practical. Nobody has to love all humanity in the abstract. You just move each ring one step closer. A cousin gets treated a bit more like a sibling, a stranger a bit more like a neighbour.

text: …to inquire of his spirit: “What bad habit of yours have you cured to-day? what vice have you checked? in what respect are you better?”
em: in what respect are you better?
author: Seneca
more:
Seneca borrowed this nightly review from the philosopher Quintus Sextius and says he does it himself. When the lamp is out, he goes over his whole day, what he said and what he did, hiding nothing from himself.

It’s where the rest of this thread becomes a habit. Each night you check where you mixed up what you control with what you don’t. Seneca says the sleep that follows is sweeter.

text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
em: I shall meet with the busybody
author: Marcus Aurelius
more:
Marcus Aurelius ran the Roman Empire, and this is how he got ready for a workday. The passage goes on: these people are his kin, made for cooperation like feet, hands and eyelids, so they can’t harm him and he can’t hate them.

He pairs two ideas. Expect friction, so it doesn’t catch you off guard. And people who behave badly usually can’t see what’s good, which makes them easier to pity than to hate.

text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
author: Marcus Aurelius
more:
By Book 10 of the Meditations, Marcus sounds fed up with himself. He’d studied with the best teachers and could describe the good life in detail. This line is him cutting off his own stalling.

Talking about virtue can feel like progress, which makes it a comfy place to hide. Marcus’s fix is three words long: but be such.

text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. … so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession.
author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
more:
Seneca opens the first of his 124 surviving letters to his friend Lucilius with this, written near the end of his life. He notices how carefully we guard money and possessions while letting others spend our hours freely. Nobody feels in debt for having taken someone’s time.

The letters were his way of teaching philosophy as a chat between friends. Nearly 2,000 years later, meetings and feeds are still ousting us from possession.

text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 13 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
more:
The letter went to a friend bracing for trouble. Many of the disasters we dread never arrive, and the ones that do rarely look how we pictured them. Meanwhile the worrying is already real suffering.

In the same letter he sorts fears into three kinds. Some things torment us more than they should, some before they should, and some when they never should at all.

text: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny … To follow I am ready. If I choose not, I make myself a wretch, and still must follow.
author: Cleanthes
source: Quoted in Epictetus, Encheiridion, 52 (trans. George Long, 1877)
more:
Cleanthes ran the Stoic school after Zeno. He’d been a boxer and paid for his studies by carrying water at night. Epictetus loved these lines enough to put them near the end of his handbook, and Seneca turned them into Latin with an extra line: fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.

In the poem the road goes where it goes either way. The only choice left is whether you walk it or get dragged.

title: The view from above
text: One habit of Marcus Aurelius: picture the earth from high above, crowded with people being born, quarrelling and dying, then find your own problem down there.
author: Marcus Aurelius
more:
Marcus comes back to this image again and again in the Meditations: crowds, voyages, feasts and quarrels, plus everyone in the past and future who’ll never know your name. The historian Pierre Hadot called it ‘the view from above’.

The point is proportion. An awkward email or a rival’s win looks tiny from high enough up, and so does the craving for praise. How you treat people still looks the same size.

title: Philosophy is for women too
text: In first-century Rome, Musonius Rufus argued women should study philosophy just like men. They have the same reason, he said, and the same natural pull toward virtue.
author: Musonius Rufus
source: Lectures, 3: That Women Too Should Study Philosophy
more:
Musonius Rufus was one of the most respected teachers in imperial Rome, and he taught Epictetus. His lectures survive in notes his students took. Two of them argue that women should study philosophy and that daughters deserve the same education as sons, a striking view for the time.

His reasoning is very Stoic. If a good life depends on reason and character, not status or the body, then everyone has what it takes. He also insisted philosophy was something you practise.

title: The obstacle is the way
text: Ryan Holiday built a whole 2014 book on one line from Marcus Aurelius: the mind turns whatever blocks it into material to work with.
author: Ryan Holiday
source: The Obstacle Is the Way (2014), drawing on Meditations, Book 5.20
more:
In Book 5 of the Meditations, Marcus notes that other people can block his actions but not his attitude. The mind turns each hindrance into an aid, so the obstacle on the road helps us along the road.

Holiday’s book retells this through stories of athletes, generals and entrepreneurs, and it helped kick off the modern Stoicism revival. Its practical question: what does this obstacle let me practise? A harsh critic, for example, is a chance at patience.

title: Philosophy as mental drills
text: Pierre Hadot argued that ancient philosophy was a training programme for the mind more than a set of theories. Stoic texts are full of repeated drills.
em: a training programme for the mind
author: Pierre Hadot
source: Philosophy as a Way of Life (1995)
more:
Hadot, a French scholar of ancient thought, noticed something odd about the Meditations. Marcus repeats himself constantly. Hadot’s explanation: Marcus was writing spiritual exercises for himself, notes to reshape his own habits of thought, the way an athlete repeats drills.

Seen that way, the repetition is the point. Understanding a Stoic idea once is easy. Living by it takes the same rehearsal as any other skill.

title: Stoicism started with a shipwreck
text: Zeno of Citium, a merchant, survived a shipwreck on the way to Athens. Around 301 BC he started teaching in the Painted Porch, the Stoa Poikile. Hence ‘Stoics’.
author: Zeno of Citium
more:
The story comes from Diogenes Laërtius, an ancient biographer, so some details may be embellished. In Athens, Zeno read about Socrates in a bookshop and asked where to find men like that. The bookseller reportedly pointed at Crates the Cynic, who happened to be walking past. Zeno became his student before founding his own school.

His followers were first called Zenonians. The name that stuck came from the porch, a painted colonnade in the Athenian marketplace.

title: Meditations was never meant for us
text: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations as private notes he never meant to publish. One old manuscript calls it ‘to himself’. Parts were written on campaign along the Danube.
em: notes he never meant to publish
author: Marcus Aurelius
more:
Marcus was emperor from 161 to 180 AD, and wrote in Greek, the language of philosophy for educated Romans. Notes in the text place Book 1 among the Quadi, a tribe he was fighting near the River Hron in modern Slovakia, and Book 2 at Carnuntum, an army base on the Danube.

So it reads less like a guru’s lecture and more like a tired, busy man reminding himself how he wants to behave.

title: Epictetus in a prison camp
text: US pilot James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam in 1965 and held for over seven years. He credited Epictetus, a former slave, with getting him through.
author: James Stockdale
more:
Stockdale was the most senior naval officer held in Hanoi, in the prison Americans called the Hanoi Hilton. He got the Medal of Honor in 1976 for his leadership as a prisoner, and later spent years at Stanford’s Hoover Institution writing and lecturing on Stoicism.

His essay Courage Under Fire: Testing Epictetus’s Doctrines in a Laboratory of Human Behavior spells it out. His captors controlled his body and his circumstances. His judgments and his will stayed his.

title: What would you still have?
text: Say a fire takes everything tonight: house, things, savings. List what you’d still have. Is that list where most of your attention goes?
author: Seneca
source: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9 (trans. Richard M. Gummere, 1917)
more:
Seneca’s answer: your character and your judgment, the things no fire can touch. He tells the story of Stilbo, a philosopher whose city was captured and whose wife and children were lost. When the conquering general Demetrius asked if he’d lost anything, Stilbo said he had all his goods with him.

He meant the things no army could carry off. The Stoics didn’t pretend losses don’t hurt. They just wanted to know what a person actually depends on.

title: Have you done it too?
text: Think of the last person who really annoyed you. Be honest: have you ever done something similar, or wanted to?
em: have you ever done something similar
author: Marcus Aurelius
more:
Marcus Aurelius assumed the answer is usually yes. In Book 11 he lists ways to cool down when someone offends him. One is to remember that you do plenty wrong too, and are a person like others. Even when you avoid a fault, he says, you often have the urge and are held back only by caution or worry about your reputation.

Most anger quietly treats the other person as a different kind of creature. Remembering your own slips brings them back to human size.
